target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection should be used in biology classes because it has educational value and reduces ethical concerns by using already-deceased specimens.
objection: AG2 argued that real-animal dissection is ethically and environmentally problematic because about 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, which harms local populations and biodiversity, and because the supply methods are inhumane.

target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is educationally justified because it is part of biology education standards or aligned with them.
objection: AG2 argued that animal dissection is not required by College Board AP Biology or the Next Generation Science Standards, so it is unnecessary for meeting formal science-education requirements.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is needed or uniquely valuable despite alternatives.
objection: AG2 argued that synthetic models and computer simulations teach just as well or better than real-animal dissection, so effective non-animal alternatives already exist.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is not educationally necessary because standards do not explicitly mandate it.
objection: AG2 disputed AG1’s attempt to infer that dissection is still appropriate from standards that set objectives rather than methods, arguing instead that not being required by AP Biology/NGSS shows it is unnecessary or should be rejected.

target: AG1’s claim that typical dissection uses already-dead byproduct specimens rather than live-captured animals.
objection: AG2 countered that the claim is not generally true because approximately 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, implying that many programs rely on live-captured animals rather than only already-deceased byproducts.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection’s educational benefits—especially fine-motor and hand-eye-coordination gains—justify using real animals.
objection: AG2 argued that tactile alternative labs using simulators and synthetic anatomy models can provide dissection-equivalent manual cutting and handling practice, so those skills do not uniquely require real-animal dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is needed for investigation-based biology learning because students must work with primary, specimen-based evidence.
objection: AG2 argued that virtual dissection software and synthetic anatomy platforms also let students actively manipulate specimens and record measurements or observations, so alternatives can generate primary, specimen-based evidence too.

target: AG1’s repeated claim that the ethical objection to dissection is weakened when specimens are already-dead byproducts such as fetal pigs destined for landfill.
objection: AG2 argued that meat-industry byproducts still come from an inhumane and environmentally harmful industrial meat-production system, so using them does not remove the ethical and environmental problems attached to real-animal dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that the educational benefits of dissection justify using it in the typical byproduct-supply scenario.
objection: AG2 argued that even if dissection has educational benefits, real-animal dissection remains ethically and environmentally problematic, and non-animal alternatives can achieve the same learning goals without using real animals.

target: AG1’s claim that real-animal dissection provides distinctive tactile, procedural, and variability-based learning not matched by alternatives.
objection: AG2 responded that synthetic models and computer simulations teach equally well or better, so the supposed distinctive benefits are not educationally necessary and can be replicated by alternatives.

target: AG1’s claim that the ethics of dissection are acceptable when using already-dead byproduct specimens rather than live-captured animals.
objection: AG2 argued that because dissection supply chains are overwhelmingly wild-capture based, the practice still carries biodiversity harms and is not merely a minor ethical exception.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives have not been shown to match dissection’s required learning outcomes without killing animals.
objection: AG2 argued that AP Biology and NGSS do not require dissection and that non-animal alternatives can meet the required learning outcomes, so the lack of a perfect match does not justify real-animal dissection.
